text: SOC Operations and SIEM Fundamentals already covered the triage loop — fire, review, classify, act — and its three outcomes: true positive, false positive, and benign true positive. Detection and Analysis, the second NIST phase, is that same discipline applied at a different scale. An alert firing is a claim that something bad might be happening. It is not, by itself, proof.

The whole purpose of Detection and Analysis is to take that claim and either confirm it as a real incident or rule it out, and when it's confirmed, to understand what kind of incident it actually is before moving into the response phases that follow. A potential incident takes more work than a single alert precisely because getting it wrong is more expensive in both directions.

An analyst or team working this phase pulls together everything triage already surfaces — the raw logs, the host or account involved, related activity nearby in time — and goes further, tracing how the activity started, what else it touched, and whether it's still ongoing right now.

Confirming an incident is real is only half the job. Ransomware encrypting file shares calls for immediate, aggressive isolation. A single compromised account quietly accessing data it shouldn't calls for a careful, quieter approach so the attacker doesn't realize they've been noticed and destroy evidence. A phishing email reported before anyone clicked may need almost no containment at all. Detection and Analysis decides which of those situations the team is actually facing.

A team too quick to declare 'incident' over everything unusual burns its own response capacity and erodes trust in its judgment next time it raises an alarm. A team too slow or too skeptical to confirm a genuine incident gives an attacker more time inside the environment, extending dwell time. Detection and Analysis exists to get that call right, using evidence rather than gut instinct. Next up: Containment, Eradication, and Recovery.
